title: Capacity to Ship Packages Within D Days
description: Brute force to optimized: sequential capacity testing versus binary search on the ship capacity, using a greedy daily-loading simulation as the feasibility check.

content.title: Capacity to Ship Packages Within D Days

blocks.text: Problem Summary: A conveyor belt has packages (given as weights, in the fixed order they must be shipped) that must be shipped within days days. Each day, the ship loads packages (in the given order, without splitting any package) up to its weight capacity. Return the MINIMUM ship capacity that allows all packages to be shipped within days days.

blocks.text: As the ship's capacity increases, the number of days needed to ship everything can only decrease or stay the same, never increase. This monotonic relationship between capacity and days needed is exactly the structure "binary search on the answer" exploits, searching directly over candidate capacities.

blocks.title: Analogy: Choosing the Smallest Truck That Still Meets a Delivery Deadline
blocks.text: Picture a fixed sequence of boxes that must be loaded onto a truck in order, without splitting any box across trips, and wanting the smallest truck capacity that still finishes within a delivery deadline of a fixed number of trips. A bigger truck always needs fewer or equal trips, so you can binary search directly on the truck's capacity.

blocks.caption: A larger ship capacity always needs fewer or equal days, a monotonic relationship enabling binary search

blocks.text: Result: 15. With capacity 15: day1=[1,2,3,4,5](15), day2=[6,7](13), day3=[8](8... wait needs recompute), the greedy packing fits within 5 days.

Before testing capacities sequentially from max(weights) upward, notice that the number of days needed (via greedy daily loading) is a monotonically non-increasing function of capacity, which is exactly the signal for binary searching directly on the candidate capacity.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: For a fixed candidate capacity, the number of days needed can be computed directly with a single greedy pass: keep adding the next package to the current day's load as long as it fits; once it does not, start a new day.

Observation 2: The minimum possible capacity is max(weights) (since no single package can be split, the capacity must at least accommodate the heaviest one), and the maximum useful capacity is sum(weights) (shipping everything in a single day).

Observation 3: As candidate capacity increases within this range, the greedy days-needed computation can only decrease or stay the same, a monotonic relationship.

Observation 4: Binary search over this range, using the greedy days-needed computation as the feasibility check (days needed <= days), converges on the minimum feasible capacity.

This leads to binary searching over candidate capacities in [max(weights), sum(weights)], computing the days needed via a greedy pass at each candidate, and narrowing toward the minimum feasible capacity.
Try capacities starting from max(weights) upward, computing the greedy days needed at each, stopping at the first capacity fitting within days days.

items: Starting from capacity = max(weights), simulate greedy daily loading and count the days needed.
If the days needed is at most "days," return this capacity.
Otherwise, increment the capacity and repeat.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Trying every capacity starting from max(weights) directly finds the smallest feasible one, guaranteed correct.
This could require up to sum(weights) - max(weights) iterations, potentially slow for large arrays with large weights.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O((sum(weights) - max(weights)) times n), checking every capacity sequentially.
Space: O(1).
Limitation: since days needed is monotonic in capacity, binary search finds the minimum feasible capacity in O(n times log(sum(weights))) instead of a full linear scan over capacities.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why sequential capacity testing is slow: with weights potentially summing into the millions, testing every capacity from max(weights) upward could take a huge number of iterations.

The binary search insight: since increasing capacity can only decrease (or keep the same) the days needed, this is a classic monotonic feasibility function, exactly the structure binary search on the answer exploits.

Defining the feasibility check: for a candidate capacity, greedily simulate loading packages day by day (adding the next package if it fits, otherwise starting a new day), and count the days used; if this is <= days, the capacity is feasible.

The core idea: binary search directly on the candidate capacity, using the greedy days-needed simulation as the feasibility check.

Binary search capacity in [max(weights), sum(weights)]. At each step, greedily simulate daily loading at that capacity, counting days needed; if <= days, move hi to the candidate (searching for a possibly smaller feasible capacity); otherwise move lo higher.

blocks.caption: Binary search on capacity, using a greedy daily-loading simulation as the feasibility check

blocks.text: Since the greedy days-needed function is monotonically non-increasing in capacity, the binary search invariant holds: if a candidate capacity is feasible (days needed <= days), a smaller capacity might still be feasible, so the search continues in the lower half (inclusive); if infeasible, every smaller capacity is also infeasible, so the search must move higher. The greedy daily-loading simulation itself is correct because packing packages in their given order, filling each day's capacity as much as possible before starting a new day, is provably optimal (any other valid packing uses at least as many days).

blocks.text: Capacity to Ship Packages Within D Days is another instance of the "binary search on the answer" template, this time with a greedy simulation as the feasibility check, showing how the same pattern reapplies across differently-worded problems.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "minimum capacity to finish within a fixed number of days/trips", think: binary search on the capacity, using a greedy simulation as the feasibility check.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Sequential capacity testing costs O((sum(weights) - max(weights)) times n) time; binary search on capacity costs O(n times log(sum(weights))) time, both using O(1) space.

items: Pattern: binary search on the answer (capacity), using a greedy daily-loading simulation as the monotonic feasibility check.
Core Idea: binary search capacity in [max(weights), sum(weights)]; greedily simulate daily loading to count days needed; narrow toward the minimum feasible capacity.
Time: O((sum(weights) - max(weights)) times n) for sequential testing, O(n times log(sum(weights))) for binary search.
Most Important Observation: capacity and days-needed have a monotonic (inverse) relationship, enabling binary search directly on the capacity.
Interview Difficulty: a very well-known "binary search on the answer" template problem, structurally identical to several others.
One line memory trick: binary search the capacity; greedily simulate daily loading as the feasibility check.
